Baby & Child

Strabismus in children: eye alignment, glasses and surgery

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Strabismus means that the eyes do not point at the same target together. It is also called a squint. An eye may turn inward, outward, upward or downward; the turn may be constant, intermittent or alternate between eyes. An examination can identify the pattern, check each eye’s sight and guide treatment. A child who does not complain can still need care.

Alignment and vision are related, but different

Eye movements depend on coordinated signals between the brain, nerves and muscles around the eyes. An alignment problem is not simply a sign that a child needs stronger eye muscles. It can affect how the brain combines information from the two eyes, including the binocular cues used to judge depth.

In young children, the brain may suppress information from the turned eye to avoid conflicting images. Vision in that eye may then develop less well: this is amblyopia. Strabismus describes alignment; amblyopia describes reduced visual development. Either can occur without the other. Older children with a new turn may report double vision, but absence of double vision does not establish normal sight.

Signs and the right time to ask for help

You may notice an eye drifting, a persistent head tilt, looking sideways or closing one eye to see. Some children close one eye in bright sunlight, particularly with an intermittent outward turn. These behaviours are clues rather than a diagnosis. Tell the clinician when the turn started, whether it comes and goes, and whether it changes with tiredness or looking near or far.

Arrange assessment for constant crossing at any age, or an intermittent turn that continues beyond three months. Brief, occasional misalignment can occur in younger babies, but persistent concerns should still be raised. Do not wait for school screening, assume the child will grow out of it, or delay because the eyes look straight during an appointment. A photograph of an occasional turn may help explain what you have seen.

Sudden changes need a different level of urgency

A newly appearing or suddenly worse squint needs urgent medical or eye-service advice. Sudden double vision, or double vision with eye pain, also needs urgent assessment. Seek emergency care if a sudden eye turn occurs with double vision, or if blurred or double vision accompanies a severe headache or an unexpectedly enlarged pupil. Double vision after a head injury is another emergency.

An eye turn with new weakness, marked imbalance, unusual drowsiness or another neurological change needs emergency assessment. A white pupil, abnormal white photographic reflection or loss of normal visual response needs immediate contact with an urgent eye or medical service. If prompt specialist assessment cannot be arranged, use emergency care. Do not wait for several warning signs together or for a routine squint appointment.

Why an eye turn can develop

The cause is not always identified. Focusing problems, family history and premature birth can be relevant. Many children with strabismus have no wider health disorder. Others have associated conditions such as cerebral palsy, Down syndrome or hydrocephalus. An eye injury, a nerve problem or poor sight from another eye condition can also disturb alignment.

Cataract can reduce the clarity of an eye’s image, while rare eye or brain disease may produce a new turn. This is why examination matters; it does not mean that most children with a squint have a tumour. Give the team the child’s birth, development and eye history. The findings determine whether additional assessment is needed, rather than an internet list of possible causes.

When eyes only appear to be crossed

A broad nasal bridge or skin folds near the inner eye corners can make a baby’s eyes look turned in even when they are aligned. This is pseudostrabismus. The appearance can become less noticeable as the face grows. A clinician uses the examination, including light-reflection and cover tests, to distinguish apparent crossing from a true turn.

Do not decide from photographs alone that a turn is harmless. Pseudostrabismus and true misalignment can coexist, and a child assessed as having pseudostrabismus can develop strabismus later. Follow the recommended reviews and report a new or changing turn. Pseudostrabismus itself does not require alignment surgery; a confirmed true turn needs its own plan.

Understanding inward and outward turns

Esotropia means inward turning. Infantile esotropia begins early in life and is not necessarily visible on the day of birth. Accommodative esotropia is a different pattern: the effort of focusing, usually in a farsighted child, contributes to crossing. “Accommodative” describes this focusing mechanism; it does not mean that the eye turn is always constant. An examination distinguishes the subtypes.

Exotropia means outward turning. It may come and go, sometimes becoming noticeable during tiredness, illness or distance viewing, or it may be constant. The specialist considers how often it occurs, how well the child regains alignment, symptoms and binocular vision. A decision about surgery depends on these findings, not simply on reaching a particular birthday. Vertical turns and other patterns also occur.

What the eye examination checks

The eye team assesses vision in each eye using age-appropriate methods, measures alignment and watches eye movements. Covering one eye at a time helps reveal a turn and how the eyes refocus. The examination also checks eye health and focusing needs; drops may be used to relax focusing for an accurate glasses measurement. Babies do not need to read a letter chart to be assessed.

An ophthalmologist, orthoptist and optometrist may contribute, depending on the service. Ask what type of turn is present, whether either eye has amblyopia and how binocular function will be followed. Share previous glasses prescriptions and photographs if useful. A screening result or a single appearance is not a substitute for the full assessment and repeat measurements when needed.

Glasses and amblyopia treatment have separate jobs

For accommodative esotropia, the prescribed glasses reduce the focusing effort that drives crossing. They are usually worn throughout the day. The eyes may still turn when the glasses are removed; this does not by itself mean the treatment has failed. Some children need a bifocal prescription for extra crossing at near. Surgery may be considered for a remaining turn with glasses on, and usually does not remove the need for them.

If amblyopia is present, the team may prescribe a patch or atropine drops for the better-seeing eye, encouraging use of the eye with weaker vision. This develops visual function rather than strengthening an eye muscle. The eye, medicine and schedule must be prescribed individually. Do not start or increase treatment independently. Alignment surgery does not replace glasses or amblyopia care that remains necessary.

Prisms, exercises and other selected options

A prism changes the direction of light through a lens and may reduce double vision in selected small misalignments. It does not cure the underlying eye-movement problem. Prescribed orthoptic exercises can help specific conditions such as convergence insufficiency, in which coordinating the eyes for near work is difficult. They are not a general treatment for every inward or outward turn.

Evidence does not support generic exercises as a cure for intermittent exotropia. Avoid programmes promising that muscle training will correct any squint or resolve learning difficulties. A specialist may sometimes offer botulinum toxin treatment, alone or alongside surgery, for a selected alignment problem. Ask why an option fits this diagnosis, what its limits are and how progress will be measured.

When muscle surgery is considered

Infantile esotropia often needs surgery, sometimes early in childhood to support use of the eyes together. Timing is individual; assessment should not wait for an arbitrary age. For other patterns, surgery may address a turn that is frequent, poorly controlled, symptomatic or insufficiently corrected by appropriate glasses. There is no requirement to try every patch, prism and exercise before an operation can be discussed.

The surgeon changes the position or length of selected muscles attached to the outside of the eyeball, working through the thin surface covering called conjunctiva. The eye is not removed from its socket. One or both eyes may be operated on, even when the turn seems more obvious on one side. Children generally have a general anesthetic and often go home the same day.

Benefits, limitations and recovery

The aim is better alignment, with possible improvement in how the eyes work together or in double vision. Normal depth perception cannot be guaranteed. A remaining or returning turn can require further treatment or another operation. Discuss risks such as persistent double vision, infection, a slipped muscle or injury to the eye; serious loss of sight is rare but possible.

Soreness and redness are common initially, and full recovery can take weeks. There is no universal return to every activity within two or three days. Follow the surgeon’s drops, hygiene, school, swimming and sport instructions and attend reviews. Contact the team urgently for worsening pain, reduced vision, increasing swelling or discharge, or severe or persistent symptoms beyond the expected recovery plan.

Follow-up and everyday support

Alignment, vision and a glasses prescription can change as a child grows. Continued checks help the team decide whether observation remains suitable or treatment needs adjustment. A straight-looking eye does not prove that amblyopia has resolved, and improved visual acuity does not necessarily mean alignment is normal. Ask for the next review date and the changes that should prompt earlier contact.

Help the child wear prescribed glasses comfortably and tell the team about practical barriers. Share agreed needs with nursery or school, and address teasing without blaming the child for an eye difference. Include the child’s views in treatment discussions when possible. The care plan should explain which problem each treatment addresses, what improvement is realistic and whom to contact with concerns.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the eye team to name the alignment subtype and explain the separate vision and binocular findings.

Keep written instructions for glasses and any prescribed amblyopia treatment, with a review date.

Before surgery, discuss which muscles or eyes will be treated, realistic benefits, risks and the individual recovery plan.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise observations and questions for the eye team. It cannot diagnose alignment from a photograph, measure a child’s sight or choose patching, drops, exercises or surgery.

When to seek help

Seek urgent advice for a new squint or sudden double vision. A sudden eye turn with double vision, double or blurred vision with severe headache or an unexpectedly enlarged pupil, double vision after head injury, or an eye turn with new neurological symptoms needs emergency care. Contact an urgent eye or medical service immediately for a white pupil or loss of visual response; use emergency care if prompt assessment is unavailable. Follow prescribed treatments and seek urgent postoperative advice for worsening pain, reduced vision or concerning swelling or discharge.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Strabismus concerns eye alignment; amblyopia concerns developing sight and may need separate treatment.
  • Constant crossing at any age or an intermittent turn beyond three months deserves assessment; raise earlier concerns too.
  • Glasses can correct focusing-related crossing, while exercises are useful only for selected diagnosed problems.
  • Muscle surgery and recovery are individual; glasses, amblyopia care and further reviews may still be needed.
  • Sudden changes, double vision with warning signs or an abnormal pupil need urgent or emergency assessment.

Frequently asked questions

What causes strabismus in a child?

Sometimes no single cause is found. Focusing errors, family history, prematurity, reduced vision or a problem affecting movement control can contribute. Many children have no wider health disorder. A new turn needs assessment rather than assuming either a harmless cause or a serious diagnosis.

How can an eye turn affect vision?

The brain may ignore one eye’s image, leading to amblyopia, and the eyes may not provide normal binocular depth information. A new turn in an older child may cause double vision. An examination measures sight and alignment separately.

Which signs should I look for?

An inward, outward or vertical turn, closing one eye, a head tilt or looking sideways can be clues. Some turns are occasional. Seek assessment even without a complaint; use urgent or emergency services for sudden changes or the warning signs described above.

How is childhood strabismus treated?

Treatment follows the subtype and measured visual needs. It may include glasses, separate amblyopia treatment, selected orthoptic care or muscle surgery. Some children are monitored. There is no single exercise or operation that suits every eye turn.

Does crossing without glasses mean surgery is needed?

Not necessarily. In accommodative esotropia, the important question includes how well the eyes align with the correct glasses on. A residual turn may need surgery, but the child may still need glasses afterwards. Keep wearing them as prescribed.

Can I treat a squint with exercises from a video?

Do not substitute a generic routine for assessment. Exercises have a role in selected diagnosed coordination problems such as convergence insufficiency, with instruction and review. They are not established treatment for all strabismus or intermittent exotropia.

Will surgery also cure lazy eye?

Not automatically. Surgery changes alignment; amblyopia may still need prescribed visual treatment. The team checks both eyes and explains whether glasses, patching or drops should continue. Better appearance alone does not measure the result for sight.

Will one operation be enough?

Sometimes, but a remaining or later returning turn may need another operation or other treatment. Recovery and long-term binocular vision vary. Ask about the expected benefit, risks and follow-up for this child rather than relying on a fixed recovery or success promise.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
